title: Haunted: The Ghost Stories of La Porte County

lines.say: On the shore of Lake Michigan, for forty-three years, a woman climbed to the same lamp every night and lit it. Some people say she still does.

v.text: the old Michigan City lighthouse, at dusk

lines.say: Inland, a former United States senator sat in the dark and listened to a drum that no one was playing.
In a La Porte cemetery, a single marker stands for four hundred and ninety-nine unknown persons.
Out in the farm country, the story goes, a chapel burned more than a hundred and fifty years ago, and was never at peace again.
And in the summer of 1905, a newspaper told of a man with no head, standing by the railroad tracks after dark, flagging down a train.
lines.tts: And in the summer of nineteen oh five, a newspaper told of a man with no head, standing by the railroad tracks after dark, flagging down a train.

lines.say: These are the ghost stories of La Porte County, Indiana.
And this is the history behind them: what's real, what's legend, and what no one can prove.

lines.say: La Porte is French for “the door.” The name is said to come from a natural opening in the forest, a doorway onto the prairie.

lines.say: For generations before any settlers came, this was Potawatomi land.

lines.say: Under treaties signed in 1826 and 1832, the Potawatomi ceded their land here to the United States. In 1838, the government forced hundreds of Potawatomi people to leave Indiana for Kansas. The march is remembered as the Trail of Death.

lines.say: A place where so much has come and gone leaves stories behind. Some are history. Some are legend. Many are a little of both.
In this film, we'll tell you which is which, as best the records allow.
In 1853, a young music teacher named Harriet Colfax moved from Ogdensburg, New York, to Michigan City, with her brother.

lines.say: Newspapers long said she owed the job to her cousin, Schuyler Colfax, a congressman from South Bend who later became vice president. She told a reporter she'd been appointed by Mr. Lincoln, soon after his inauguration.

lines.say: Every evening, she lit the lamps. At first they burned lard oil. She heated it on the stove, and on cold nights it could harden again before she got it to the light.

In 1871, a second light was built out on the pier, at the end of a long, raised wooden walkway. In 1874, it was moved to the west pier, across Trail Creek. To reach it, she rowed across the creek in a small boat.

lines.say: She kept the light for forty-three years. People called her Old Faithful.

v.cap: keeper of the Michigan City light, 1861 – 1904

lines.say: She didn't keep it alone. Ann Hartwell, a teacher she had known in Ogdensburg, followed her to Michigan City and lived with her at the lighthouse. The National Park Service calls Ann her lifelong companion.
Ann taught in the public schools for about twenty-five years, then opened a book exchange that became the area's first lending library.

lines.say: A Chicago newspaper quoted her: I could not bear to see anyone else light my lamp.

lines.say: Six days later, the light in the old lighthouse was put out for good. The lantern came off the roof, and a new light took its place at the end of the pier.
Harriet and Ann moved into a new home. In January, Ann died. That April, Harriet died too.

rows: Both are buried at Greenwood Cemetery.

The old lighthouse has been a museum since 1973, run by the Michigan City Historical Society.
lines.tts: The old lighthouse has been a museum since nineteen seventy-three, run by the Michigan City Historical Society.

lines.say: And it's said to have a ghost. In 2026, a boating magazine wrote that the lighthouse is said to be haunted by its keeper, still on duty. Even the magazine admitted no one knows for sure.

lines.say: We couldn't find anyone who says they've seen her. Only the story: that after forty-three years, she still can't bear to see anyone else light her lamp.
In downtown Michigan City stands the Barker Mansion.
lines.lower: Barker Mansion | 631 Washington St., Michigan City

lines.say: John H. Barker ran the Haskell and Barker Car Company, which built thousands of railroad freight cars a year. In 1905, he turned his family's home into a mansion of thirty-eight rooms.
lines.tts: John H. Barker ran the Haskell and Barker Car Company, which built thousands of railroad freight cars a year. In nineteen oh five, he turned his family's home into a mansion of thirty-eight rooms.

v.text: Haskell & Barker car works, old postcard

lines.say: The family knew grief. In 1886, Barker built a hall at Trinity Episcopal Church in memory of three children, all of whom had died as babies.
lines.tts: The family knew grief. In eighteen eighty-six, Barker built a hall at Trinity Episcopal Church in memory of three children, all of whom had died as babies.

lines.say: A marker at the mansion says both of Catherine Barker's parents died in 1910. She was fourteen, and, the marker says, the world's richest heiress.
lines.tts: A marker at the mansion says both of Catherine Barker's parents died in nineteen ten. She was fourteen, and, the marker says, the world's richest heiress.

lines.say: Victorians lived close to death, and they had rules for it. Clocks were stopped at the hour of a death. Mirrors were covered. Families wore black, sometimes for years, and had photographs taken of the dead.
This fall, the mansion is offering candlelight tours about those Victorian superstitions. But the museum is clear about what they are not.
This is not a haunted house, paranormal investigation, or ghost tour.

lines.say: Fifty years earlier, though, some people in La Porte believed they could do more than mourn the dead. They believed they could talk with them.
In the spring of 1848, two young sisters in Hydesville, New York, said they could talk with a spirit through rapping sounds. Within a few years, Spiritualism had spread across the country.
lines.tts: In the spring of eighteen forty-eight, two young sisters in Hydesville, New York, said they could talk with a spirit through rapping sounds. Within a few years, Spiritualism had spread across the country.

lines.say: Believers sat in circles in darkened rooms, hands on a table, and waited for the dead to answer.
By the mid-1850s, according to the Indiana Historical Bureau, Spiritualism was fairly widespread in Indiana.
lines.tts: By the mid-eighteen fifties, according to the Indiana Historical Bureau, Spiritualism was fairly widespread in Indiana.

lines.say: Charles W. Cathcart was one of La Porte County's leading men. Born on the island of Madeira in 1809, he had served in the Indiana Senate, in Congress, and, briefly, in the United States Senate.
lines.tts: Charles W. Cathcart was one of La Porte County's leading men. Born on the island of Madeira in eighteen oh nine, he had served in the Indiana Senate, in Congress, and, briefly, in the United States Senate.

lines.say: He was a skeptic. When he heard about a spirit circle at the home of a Mr. Poston, in La Porte County, he went to expose it.
He brought along a homemade device that could light up the dark room in a flash.
The lights went out. A spirit the circle called Old King took up a bass drum.
Cathcart set off his flash.
He described what he saw in the Spiritual Telegraph, a Spiritualist newspaper in New York: the stick beating the drum, as if handled from above, with no mortal nearer than about eight feet of it.

v.text: no mortal nearer than about eight feet of it
v.by: Charles W. Cathcart, in the Spiritual Telegraph

lines.say: What a picture for an artist, he wrote.

v.text: What a picture for an artist!
v.by: Charles W. Cathcart, in the Spiritual Telegraph

lines.say: The skeptic started holding circles of his own, and they were even livelier: flying furniture, voices with no bodies, and spirits playing music in the dark.
In 1859, a national directory of Spiritualists listed them by name: Cathcart's Spirit Rooms, Laporte.
lines.tts: In eighteen fifty-nine, a national directory of Spiritualists listed them by name: Cathcart's Spirit Rooms, Laporte.

lines.say: And in 1870, in her history of American Spiritualism, the medium Emma Hardinge gave them a chapter of their own: Cathcart's Spirit Room.
lines.tts: And in eighteen seventy, in her history of American Spiritualism, the medium Emma Hardinge gave them a chapter of their own: Cathcart's Spirit Room.

lines.say: Today, no one knows exactly where the spirit rooms stood. Charles Cathcart died in 1888, on his farm near La Porte. He's buried at Pine Lake Cemetery.
lines.tts: Today, no one knows exactly where the spirit rooms stood. Charles Cathcart died in eighteen eighty-eight, on his farm near La Porte. He's buried at Pine Lake Cemetery.

lines.say: Pine Lake Cemetery, in La Porte, was established in 1856. Its first burial was two years later.
lines.tts: Pine Lake Cemetery, in La Porte, was established in eighteen fifty-six. Its first burial was two years later.

v.text: Pine Lake, La Porte, old postcard

lines.say: Graves from the town's old city cemetery were moved here.
Not all of them had names. A marker there stands for four hundred and ninety-nine unknown persons, moved from an older burial ground.
Accounts disagree about when it happened. One says 1871. Another, 1893.
lines.tts: Accounts disagree about when it happened. One says eighteen seventy-one. Another, eighteen ninety-three.

lines.say: All that digging left a story behind. When one old coffin was opened, the story goes, the woman inside was found upside down and twisted, as if she had been buried alive.
No record of it has been found. Stories like it are told about old cemeteries all over the world.
Visitors tell of something else: shadows, like mist, above the stones.
Elsewhere in La Porte is Patton Cemetery, started in 1841.
lines.tts: Elsewhere in La Porte is Patton Cemetery, started in eighteen forty-one.

lines.say: Andrew Helgelien, the last known victim of Belle Gunness, is buried there. His story is in our last documentary.
lines.lower: Andrew Helgelien's grave | on a 1908 postcard

lines.say: A neighbor once told of hearing voices in the cemetery at night, and looking out to find no one there.

This year, the trouble at Patton has been the weather. The derecho of August eleventh, 2026, brought gusts near sixty miles an hour to La Porte. Afterward, the historical society said the cemetery was unsafe for the public to enter, and canceled its October tour.

lines.say: In the farm country northeast of La Porte, in Galena Township, there's a small cemetery called Posey Chapel.
In 2011, when a local newspaper counted down the county's ten most haunted places, Posey Chapel was number one.
lines.tts: In twenty eleven, when a local newspaper counted down the county's ten most haunted places, Posey Chapel was number one.

v.cap: La Porte County's most haunted, by one 2011 count

lines.say: The legend, as it's told online: the church burned more than a hundred and fifty years ago, and its preacher took his own life near the gate.
Since then, people say, there have been lights in the trees, red eyes, a woman in white, and on some nights, the sound of a woman singing.
Here's what the records say.
A Methodist congregation was founded here in 1833, a year after the county itself.
lines.tts: A Methodist congregation was founded here in eighteen thirty-three, a year after the county itself.

lines.say: The cemetery began as a family plot. It takes its name from Ida Posey, who, by one account, helped build a chapel here in 1841.
lines.tts: The cemetery began as a family plot. It takes its name from Ida Posey, who, by one account, helped build a chapel here in eighteen forty-one.

v.head: POSEY CHAPEL
rows: 1841: a chapel, built with Ida Posey's help.

lines.say: By the same account, the chapel burned and was rebuilt in 1855. So, by that account, there really was a fire more than a hundred and fifty years ago.
lines.tts: By the same account, the chapel burned and was rebuilt in eighteen fifty-five. So, by that account, there really was a fire more than a hundred and fifty years ago.

lines.say: And there was another. In 1972, the church burned again, and this time it wasn't rebuilt. One writer says the fire was set on purpose.
lines.tts: And there was another. In nineteen seventy-two, the church burned again, and this time it wasn't rebuilt. One writer says the fire was set on purpose.

v.cap: the church burns again; it is not rebuilt

lines.say: Today, a pavilion stands where the chapel stood, among hundreds of graves.
As for the preacher, we found no record that any preacher there took his own life, and no record of anyone dying in either fire.
It's still an active cemetery, where families bury their own. If you go, go by day, and leave it as you found it.
On July thirty-first, 1905, the Muncie Evening Press ran a story about a ghost in La Porte County, under the headline Headless Ghost Grows Uneasy.
lines.tts: On July thirty-first, nineteen oh five, the Muncie Evening Press ran a story about a ghost in La Porte County, under the headline Headless Ghost Grows Uneasy.

lines.say: It told of a place near La Porte called Flaherty's Siding, where, after dark, a figure had been seen on the railroad platform.

v.text: a small railroad station / platform, about 1905

lines.say: It had no head. It carried a dinner pail, and it swung its arms as if it were flagging an approaching train.
Then it would vanish, often with a shriek.
Headless, the paper said, and acting for all the world like an animate thing.

v.text: Headless, and acting for all the world like an animate thing

lines.say: People believed it was Columbus Cole, a well-known local man who had been run over by an engine, close to the spot where the water tank stood. The accident, the paper said, had taken his head.
Some young men from town decided it was a hoax, and went out to prove it.
The first night, they saw nothing.
On the second night, one of them called for quiet. There, near the old water tank, stood the headless figure. They watched it for five minutes or more.

v.text: water tank by the tracks, night

lines.say: Then they ran to the spot. It was gone.
By one account, they recognized the dinner pail: the one Cole always carried to and from work. We were no longer skeptics, the paper quoted them, but believers.

v.text: We were no longer skeptics, but believers.

lines.say: We tried to find Columbus Cole. We couldn't find a record of his death, which railroad it was, or even where Flaherty's Siding was. If you know, tell us in the comments.
And if you go looking, stay off the tracks. Trains still run through La Porte County, and they don't stop for ghosts.

v.text: La Porte railroad depot, old postcard

lines.say: In the fall of 1940, before the United States entered the Second World War, the government picked farmland south of La Porte for an ammunition plant.
lines.tts: In the fall of nineteen forty, before the United States entered the Second World War, the government picked farmland south of La Porte for an ammunition plant.

lines.say: It took in more than thirteen thousand acres. About two hundred and fifty families had to leave their homes and farms.
The Kingsbury Ordnance Plant made fuses for ammunition, up to a hundred and eighty thousand a day.
In May 1942, it employed twenty thousand, seven hundred and eighty-five people. Nearly half of them were women.
lines.tts: In May nineteen forty-two, it employed twenty thousand, seven hundred and eighty-five people. Nearly half of them were women.

v.cap: workers, May 1942; nearly half of them women

lines.say: To house them, builders started nearly three thousand homes in a new town, laid out in a circle like a wagon wheel. At first, it was called Victory City. Today it's Kingsford Heights.
The work was dangerous. An explosive called tetryl turned some workers' skin orange.
In that 2011 list of the county's most haunted places, the plant was number ten. The writer said she'd been told that explosions had killed workers there during the war.
lines.tts: In that twenty eleven list of the county's most haunted places, the plant was number ten. The writer said she'd been told that explosions had killed workers there during the war.

lines.say: We found no record of deadly explosions there. One writer who researched the plant says there were never any major accidents.
The plant closed after the war, reopened for the Korean War, and closed for good around 1960.
lines.tts: The plant closed after the war, reopened for the Korean War, and closed for good around nineteen sixty.

lines.say: In 1965, much of the land went to the state. Today it's the Kingsbury Fish and Wildlife Area, where people hunt, fish and hike.
lines.tts: In nineteen sixty-five, much of the land went to the state. Today it's the Kingsbury Fish and Wildlife Area, where people hunt, fish and hike.

lines.say: Other parts of the old plant are private industrial land, and off-limits. If you go, stay on public land, and wear orange in hunting season.
Sometimes a place feels haunted simply because so much happened there, and so few people remember.
Most of these stories can't be proved. Some can be disproved.

But the people in them were real. A keeper who climbed to her lamp for forty-three years. A senator who sat in the dark and listened. Four hundred and ninety-nine people no one could name. A congregation that lost its church. A railroad man named Columbus Cole. And twenty thousand workers who went to war without leaving home.
Maybe that's what a ghost story is: a way of remembering.
The Old Lighthouse Museum is open Wednesday through Sunday afternoons until the end of October.
The cemeteries are active, and they belong to the families. Go by day, be respectful, and stay off private land.
